abstract: Background Multiple myeloma (MM), the second most prevalent hematological malignancy, carries high morbidity with variability in clinical progression among patients. This necessitates accurate risk stratification for effective therapy and life planning. While extensively genomically and transcriptomically characterized, MM remains modestly studied from a proteomic perspective. As proteomics is a closer measure of phenotype than genomic and transcriptomic assessments, addressing this gap in the literature may yield new insights into disease biology and novel biomarkers. Methods Herein, we applied a new sample preparation approach for mass-spectrometry based proteomics to bone marrow interstitial fluid (BMIF) from patients with MM or its precursors. Results We achieved deep coverage of the proteome, identifying > 11,000 protein groups (PGs) across our cohort, with an average of ~ 8900 PGs per sample. Of these, 194 PGs were significantly associated with overall survival (OS). These survival-associated PGs were enriched for those involved in coagulation, and clustering newly diagnosed MM (NDMM) based on coagulation-related proteins revealed three distinct groups characterised by globally high, medium, and low intensity of coagulation-related proteins. The group with low intensity of coagulation-related PGs had significantly reduced OS (log-rank p = 0.00078). Clustering was independent of measured clinical covariates, including chemotherapeutic regimens used, Revised International Staging System (R-ISS stage), International Normalised Ratio (INR), and age, among others. Conclusion Our findings support the value of fluid-based proteomic assessment of MM and suggest that coagulation-related PGs could serve as valuable novel biomarkers for risk stratification in multiple myeloma, warranting further investigation into this area. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12014-025-09560-6.
methods:
Methods
Sample collection
BMIF samples were taken from 117 plasma cell dyscrasia patients, of which 80 had newly diagnosed MM (NDMM), 18 had relapsed or refractory MM (RRMM), and 19 had preclinical/low plasma cell burden disease [8 MGUS, 8 SMM, 1 with monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS); 1 with polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy, skin changes (POEMS); 1 with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma]. Sample collection and processing are as described previously [
29
]. Matching clinical data was collected for each patient and deposited in a REDCap database administered through the Terry Fox Research Institute. All collection and use of human samples were conducted in accordance with the declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Nova Scotia Health Authority institutional review board (REB# 1021397, 1022793 and 1021520). All patients provided written informed consent.
Proteomic workflow
BMIF samples were sent for processing at Seer™ (Redwood, CA) using their standard Proteograph-XT™ protocol for generating tryptic peptides [
21
]. These samples were randomized prior to sending to Seer™ to minimize batch effects, and Seer™ was blinded to the disease type of each sample. Sample preparation was performed robotically, minimizing assay noise. Briefly, each sample was aliquoted into two wells on 96 well plates. Each aliquot was then mixed with one of the two proprietary and commercially available nanoparticles (NP-A, NP-B) used in the Proteograph-XT™ assay such that for each sample there was an aliquot mixed with one of each nanoparticle. Aliquot-nanoparticle mixtures were incubated for one hour to allow for stable corona formation. These nanoparticles were subsequently precipitated, the supernatant removed, and washed three times in buffer solution. Then coronas were reduced, alkylated, and digested with trypsin.
Alongside the 117 experimental samples, four technical controls (process control 1 and 2, digestion control, and clean-up control) were run on each 96 well plate as part of the Proteograph-XT™ assay, for a total of 12 controls across the experiment. Process controls 1 and 2 are pooled Seer™ plasma samples that are incubated with NP-A and NP-B, respectively, and exposed to every step of the assay. The digestion control is exposed to the trypsin digestion and peptide cleanup steps. The clean-up control is a purified mixture of commercially available pre-digested peptides exposed only to the clean-up step.
The resultant peptides were analysed via liquid chromatography coupled mass spectrometry (LC–MS) in data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode performed on a Thermo Scientific Vanquish NEO nanoLC system (400 ng injection, 1000 nL/min, 24 min gradient) (RRID:SCR_014477) coupled Thermo Fisher Orbitrap Astral (RRID:SCR_026205) tandem mass spectrometer using a trap-and-elute configuration. The trap column was an Acclaim™ PepMap™ 100 C18 (0.3 mm ID × 5 mm) and the analytic column was a Gen1 50 cm µPACTM (Thermo Scientific). Samples were separated on the analytic column at a flow rate of 1µL/min using a gradient of 4–35% mobile phase B comprised of 0.1% formic acid and 100% acetonitrile mixed into mobile phase A comprised of 0.1% formic acid and 100% water over 21 minutes, for a total run time of 26 minutes. MS1 scans were performed with a 5 ms ion injection time or 500% AGC (500,000 ion) target at 240,000 R every 0.6 s in the Orbitrap detector. At the Astral detector, the 380Th-980Th mass range was covered by 200 fixed DIA windows per cycle with 3 Th precursor isolation windows, 5 ms ion injection times with 500% (50,000 ion) active gain control maximum, and 25% normalized collision energy. MS2 scans were collected from 150–2000 m/z, and window placement optimization was turned on. A source voltage of 1500 V was used, and the ion transfer tube temperature was 300˚ C. Aliquots were run over two mass spectrometers, such that all peptides arising from NP-A were run on one instrument, and all peptides arising from NP-B were run on another instrument. Mass spectra were analysed with DIA-NN (v1.8.1, RRID:SCR_022865) in the Proteograph Analysis Suite (PAS), an online platform from Seer™.
An initial pilot study was conducted utilizing 20 BMIF samples from the full cohort, processed in a single run and analyzed as described above. These samples were later reprocessed and reanalyzed alongside the full cohort to confirm the reproducibility of our findings.
Data analysis
Unless specified otherwise, analysis was performed in R (v4.4.1, RRID:SCR_001905) [
30
].
Analysis of LCMS data
Mass spectra were analysed with DIA-NN (1.8.1) in the Proteograph Analysis Suite (PAS), an online platform from Seer™. The parameters were a False Discovery Rate (FDR) of 0.01 (peptide and protein), min peptide length of 7, max missed cleavages of 1, enzyme was set to trypsin, fixed mods were Carbamidomethyl, variable mods were Oxidation (M) and Acetyl (Protein N-term), match between runs was enabled, and the Uniprot database (RRID:SCR_002380) UP000005640_9606 (Homo sapiens) was used for library-free search [
31
]. For protein groups (PGs) identified on both nanoparticles, the PG intensity from the nanoparticle with the highest median intensity of that PG across all samples was used.
Assessing batch effect
Batch effects across plates were assessed for in the experimental samples by both visual inspection of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) plots for mixing of samples across plates, and PVCA (RRID:SCR_001356) [
32
]. The technical controls were also used to assess for batch effects by 1) visual inspection of PCA plots for segregation by control type rather than plate, and 2) assessing the coefficient of variation of PG counts and intensities across plates. In addition, PVCA was used to assess for the pre-analytical impact of sample storage duration prior to processing at Seer™ (grouped to the nearest year increment).
Differential intensity analysis
Differential intensity analysis was conducted using PAS. Only PGs with less than 25% missingness (observed in > 75% of patients) in both comparison groups were included. Their intensities were then median normalized, and protein intensity comparisons between the groups were conducted using the T-test. P values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and significant PGs were those with p < 0.05 after correction.
Survival assessment
The association of each PG’s intensity and overall and progression-free survival in NDMM patients was assessed using the Cox proportional hazard model implemented in the R package, survival (RRID:SCR_021137) [
33
]. This was performed on the set of PGs with complete data (observed in 100% of patients), and on the imputed data set which included PGs with less than 25% missingness (observed in > 75% of patients) to support that findings from the complete data set were not skewed by missingness. Prior to calculating hazard, the intensities for the PGs with complete data were variance stabilization normalized using the DEP R package (RRID:SCR_023090) [
34
]. Imputed Intensities for PGs with less than 25% missingness were calculated using the Bayesian principal component analysis (bpca) method implemented in the DEP R package [
34
]. Survival analysis between groups was conducted using Kaplan–Meier, implemented in the R package, survival [
33
]. P values were corrected for multiple testing using Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, with significant PGs identified as those with p < 0.05 after correction.
Gene set and pathway enrichment analysis
PGs significantly associated with survival through hazard assessment or differential intensity analysis were included in this analysis. These significant PGs were split into those associated with poor outcomes and those associated with favourable outcomes. Each list of PGs was then assessed for enrichment in Gene Set Ontology terms or WikiPathways using the R package, clusterProfiler (v4.12.2, RRID:SCR_016884) [
35
].
Patient clustering and clinical comparisons
Variance stabilized PG intensities were Z-scored within each PG, and patients were hierarchically clustered using the Ward D2 implementation on Euclidian distance. Clusters were determined by visual inspection, and dendograms were cut accordingly. For the coagulation clusters, assessment for associations with continuous clinical covariates were performed using the Wilcoxon test, and associations with categorical clinical covariates, including RISS group, pre-treatment therapies, and chemotherapy classes, were evaluated using Chi-Square test. P values were corrected for multiple testing using Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and significance was defined as p < 0.05 after correction. Prognostic independence of the coagulation-based clusters was analysed using a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model.
Data visualisations were produced with ggplot2 (v3.5.1, RRID:SCR_014601) and ComplexHeatmap (v2.20.0, RRID:SCR_017270) [
36
,
37
].

Background
Multiple Myeloma is the second most common hematological malignancy worldwide, with an increasing incidence [
1
–
3
]. It originates from a transformed post-germinal-center plasma cell clone that invades the bone marrow, progressing through a spectrum of plasma cell dyscrasias that include monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), smoldering MM (SMM), overt MM, and finally plasma cell leukemia (PCL) [
4
,
5
]. Despite significant therapeutic advancements over the past decade, MM continues to be associated with substantial morbidity and mortality [
3
,
6
–
8
]. Common clinical sequelae of MM include cytopenias/anaemia, cortical bone destruction, hypercalcemia, and renal damage.
Current clinical work-up for MM involves imaging for lytic lesions and standard blood tests to assess classic tumor markers and organ damage. Additionally, bone marrow (BM) biopsies and aspirates are essential at diagnosis and several points throughout the disease course to assess disease burden and perform cytogenetic profiling for prognostication and staging according to the Revised International Staging System (R-ISS/R2-ISS) [
9
,
10
]. These inputs have been validated by decades of research on MM’s genomic and transcriptomic patterns. However, their prognostic power has remained relatively static, with minimal advancements since their inception [
11
–
16
].
In contrast to the extensively studied genome and transcriptome of MM, its proteome has only recently begun to be investigated in depth. This delay is partly due to the technical challenges associated with proteomic characterization of large clinical cohorts [
17
]. However, technological advances have now ameliorated these hurdles, enabling large-scale, deep-proteomic assessment [
18
–
21
]. Since proteomic assessment provides a closer measure of phenotype than transcriptomics or genomics, characterizing MM at this level may reveal new disease biology and biomarkers.
Indeed, several recent proteomic studies investigating MM cells, cell surfaces, BMIF, and peripheral blood plasma (PBP) have yielded promising findings. Studies employing parallel proteomic analysis on both BMIF and PBP have identified numerous proteins differentially expressed between MM and normal samples, including several linked to coagulation pathways [
22
,
23
]. Other studies have identified higher levels of plasma cell-associated proteins in PBP of MM patients compared to healthy controls, providing insights into peripheral biomarkers for the disease. Additionally, proteogenomic profiling of plasma cells has identified risk markers that are independent of R-ISS stage [
24
–
27
]. Research into the cell surface proteome of MM cell lines has further uncovered proteins associated with treatment resistance or responsiveness [
28
].
More recent advancements in sample preparation and data analysis workflows for mass-spectrometry-based proteomics have further increased the depth of the resolvable proteome. Enhanced sensitivity, reproducibility, and scalability have been achieved through streamlined protocols utilizing e.g. nanoparticle-based methods, and automation has reduced sample loss and enabled high-throughput processing. Moreover, data-independent acquisition (DIA) and modern search algorithms allow deeper proteome coverage and more consistent quantification [
18
–
21
]. In this study, we employ an innovative nanoparticle-based sample preparation technique that was originally designed to increase the depth of mass-spectrometry proteomic experiments on peripheral blood plasma, to BMIF from MM patients for the first time [
18
–
21
]. Our objective was to deeply profile the BMIF of MM to expand our understanding of MM and identify novel biomarkers that enable independent risk stratification in this malignancy, potentially transforming patient prognosis and treatment strategies.

Results
Patient demographics
The clinical characteristics of our cohort are described in Table
1
and Supplementary Table S1. For our NDMM patients, the mean follow-up time was 35.1 months, with a range of 1.23 to 88.4 months. Pharmacotherapy used by patients at the time of diagnosis, as well as the chemotherapies used over the course of follow-up for NDMM patients are reported in Supplementary Tables S2 and S3. Patients received various regimens that included alkylating agents, glucocorticoids, proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies, and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT). The most common regimens over the follow-up period were CyBorD (Cyclophosphamide, Bortezomib, and Dexamethasone, N = 41); RD (Lenalidomide and Dexamethasone, N = 30); Lenalidomide alone (N = 23); and DRD (Daratumumab, Lenalidomide, and Dexamethasone, N = 16) (Supplementary Table S3). The most common first-line regimens were CyBorD (N = 38), RD (N = 16), DRD (N = 6), VRD (Bortezomib, Lenalidomide and Dexamethasone, N = 9) (Table
1
). Thirty patients received an ASCT during the follow-up period (Table
1
).

Table reporting summarized clinical characteristics. The section summarizing first line treatment regimens includes only common therapies across the cohort. (RD: Lenalidomide, Dexamethasone; DRD: Daratumumab, Lenalidomide, Dexamethasone; VRD: Bortezomib, Lenalidomide, Dexamethasone).
Minimal batch effect
Experimental samples demonstrate mixing between plates in PCA space (Supplementary Figure S1A). As well, control samples tightly clustered by type rather than plate in PCA space (Supplementary Figure S1B). Technical replicates of control samples across plates demonstrated consistency in PG counts with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 3.34% to 15.6%, and PG intensity with a CV of 2.99% to 3.91% (Supplementary Figure S1C,D). PVCA revealed that duration of sample storage, plate on which samples were processed, and the two-way interaction of these variables accounted for approximately 11% of observed variance, with ~ 89% of the variance remaining residual after accounting for these covariates (Supplementary Figure S1E).
PG count similar among plasma cell dyscrasias
We identified a total of 11,128 PGs across our patient cohort, with an average of 8976 PGs per sample (Supplementary Figure S2A; Supplementary Table S4). Out of these, 4194 PGs were common to every patient, and 7849 PGs were common to at least 75% of patients (Supplementary Figure S2B). No association was found between diagnosis and the number of PGs identified (Supplementary Figure S2A).
Plasma cell-associated proteins in BMIF show greater intensity in BMIF of NDMM compared to SMM and MGUS patients
In our comparison of NDMM to MGUS patients, we identified 28 PGs with differential intensity (Supplementary Table S5). Of these 28 PGs, seven (SH2B2, IRF4, SDC1, TNFRSF17, ISG20, CXCR4, PRKCZ) were significantly more intense in NDMM than in MGUS, while 21 were significantly more intense in MGUS. (Fig.
1
A). When comparing NDMM to SMM patients, 6 PGs showed differential intensity, with only one (SDC1) being more intense in NDMM (Fig.
1
B; Supplementary Table S6). Many of the PGs that were more intense in NDMM compared to MGUS or SMM were known plasma cell markers, such as IRF4, SDC1, and TNFRSF17. The intensities of these proteins were significantly correlated with bone marrow plasma cell burden (Supplementary Figure S3).

Risk associated BMIF PGs are enriched for coagulation
To identify prognostic signals in our proteomic data, we analyzed the association between overall survival (OS) and the intensity of each PG in NDMM samples. Initially, considering only PGs common to all NDMM samples, we identified 56 PGs associated with increased OS and 34 PGs associated with decreased OS (Fig.
2
A; Supplementary Table S7). When we expanded our analysis to include PGs with up to 25% missingness, using BPCA to estimate PG intensity, we identified 85 PGs associated with increased survival and 109 PGs associated with reduced OS (Fig.
2
B; Supplementary Table S8). These PGs spanned the intensity dynamic range (Supplementary Figure S4). Clustering patients based on the Z-scored intensity of the OS-associated PGs from the complete dataset revealed three groups with significantly different OS and progression-free survival (PFS) (Fig.
2
C-E). Differential intensity analysis comprising the 15 longest- and 15 shortest-surviving NDMM patients identified 346 PGs associated with longer OS and 128 PGs associated with shorter OS (Supplementary Figure S5, Supplemental Table S9).

Among the PGs with significantly low hazard (HR < 0.5, p < 0.05) from both the complete and imputed datasets, as well as the PGs associated with long OS from the differential intensity analysis, coagulation (GO:0007596, WP558) was the most significantly enriched Gene Ontology term/Wikipathway (Fig.
3
A-B; Supplementary Figure S6A-D; Supplemental Tables S10-21). Considering the PGs with significantly high hazard (HR > 2, p < 0.05), a mix of terms were identified, with less consistency between the analyses that included “chromosome segregation”, “ribosome biogenesis”, and “mRNA processing”, among others (Supplemental Tables S10-21). The proteins within the "Blood Coagulation" Gene Ontology term that were significantly associated with OS included coagulation factors 2, 7, 9, and 12, as well as KLKB1, SERPINA10, SERPIND1, SERPINC1, PROC, PROZ, and HGFAC. Given the prominence of the coagulation cascade in these results, we clustered our NDMM patients based on proteins within this cascade (F2, F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13A1, F13B, VWF, KLKB1, KLK1, FGA, FGB, FGG) as indicated on WikiPathways (WP272). This identified three distinct groups characterized by globally low (group 1), medium (group 2), and high (group 3) intensity of coagulation factors, with significantly different OS (log-rank p = 0.00078) and PFS (log-rank p = 0.017) (Fig.
4
A-C). The group with the worst outcome (group 1, N = 26) was characterized by low intensity of all coagulation factors and had a median survival of 16.2 months. Conversely, the group with the best outcome (group 3, N = 24) had a high intensity of all factors and a median survival of 67.2 months.

In PCA space, considering all PGs, coagulation group assignments clustered together, and a comparator group consisting of MGUS (N = 8), MGRS (N = 1), and POEMS syndrome (N = 1), largely projected amongst coagulation group 3 (Supplementary Figure S7A). This comparator group was selected due to its low plasma cell burden and relatively normal bone marrow histology. We performed differential intensity analysis comparing each of coagulation groups 1 and 3 to the comparator group. Comparing coagulation group 1 to this group identified 190 PGs significantly more intense in MM coagulation group 1 and 295 PGs significantly more intense in the comparator group (Supplementary Figure S7B; Supplementary Table S22). The PGs that were significantly more intense in MM coagulation group 1 included all PGs found to be more intense in NDMM compared to MGUS (Fig.
1
A, Supplementary Figure S7B). Comparing MM coagulation group 3 to this group identified 102 PGs significantly more intense in MM coagulation group 3 and 359 PGs significantly more intense in the comparator group (Supplementary Figure S7C; Supplementary Table S23). Of the PGs significantly more intense in the whole NDMM cohort compared to MGUS, all but CXCR4 were significantly more intense in coagulation group 3 MM (Supplementary Figure S7C). Overall, 481 PGs were differentially intense between coagulation group 1 MM and the comparator group, while 465 PGs were differentially intense between coagulation group 3 MM and the comparator group. Notably, coagulation factors 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13B, FGA, FGB, FGG, and KLKB1 were significantly less intense in coagulation group 1 compared to the comparator group (Supplementary Figure S7D). Conversely, the only coagulation cascade PG significantly differentially intense in coagulation group 3 MM compared to the comparator group was von Willebrand factor (VWF), which was more intense in coagulation group 3 (Log2FC = 0.99) (Supplementary Figure S7D). Additionally, several anticoagulant proteins were also significantly more intense in MM coagulation group 3 compared to MM coagulation group 1 or the comparator group, including PROC, PROS1, PROZ, SERPINC1, SERPINA6, SERPINCA10, SERPINI1, and SERPIND1 (Supplementary Figure S8). Finally, coagulation-regulating extracellular matrix proteins (ECM) FN1 and TNC were also significantly less intense in MM coagulation group 1 compared to MM coagulation group 3 (Supplementary Figure S9).
Coagulation biomarkers in BMIF are independent of prognostic indicators
To evaluate whether the prognostic value of coagulation clusters is independent of current clinical evaluations, we first analyzed the hazard associated with coagulation cluster assignment using a multivariate Cox model. This model accounted for R-ISS stage, age, bone marrow plasma cell burden, monoclonal (M)-protein quantity, and platelet count. The coagulation cluster assignment remained significant (HR = 0.39, p = 0.002) and outperformed the R-ISS staging (Fig.
5
A). Next, we assessed for associations between coagulation clusters and various clinical and biochemical parameters, including age at diagnosis, plasma levels of albumin, beta-2 microglobulin, creatinine and eGFR, INR, PTT, M-protein, the ratio of involved to uninvolved serum free light chains, bone marrow plasma cell burden, and platelet count; no significant associations were found (p > 0.05) (Fig.
5
B). Finally, we applied the coagulation clustering to patients staged by R-ISS and identified high- and low-risk groups within R-ISS stage 2 patients (n = 54, log-rank p = 0.021). There were too few patients in RISS stages 1 (n = 4) and 3 (n = 9) for meaningful analysis (Fig.
5
C).

We also investigated potential associations between coagulation cluster assignment and the use of anticoagulants, antiplatelets, antiglycemics, antihypertensives, or antilipidemics at the time of diagnosis. No significant associations were observed (Supplementary Figure S10A-D). Finally, we assessed for associations between coagulation group and the use of chemotherapeutic classes and ASCTs over the follow-up period; no associations were found (Figure S10E).
Discussion
We analyzed the proteome of BMIF of 117 patients, generating a dataset of over 11,000 PGs across our cohort of plasma cell dyscrasias. To our knowledge, this analysis offers one of the deepest characterizations of MM BMIF to date. Prior studies have reported significantly lower proteomic coverage, including Chanukuppa et al., who identified approximately 1,600 proteins in MM BMIF, Lightbody et al., who profiled 3,072 proteins in MM blood plasma, and Apipongrat et al., who identified 1,738 proteins [
22
,
25
,
27
]. Our analysis therefore offers the deepest coverage of BMIF reported via nanoparticle-based techniques. Importantly, we identified PGs associated with clinical hazards across a wide dynamic range, underscoring the importance of deep proteomic profiling in uncovering novel biomarkers and advancing our understanding of MM pathophysiology.
Batch effects are important confounders in mass spectrometry based proteomic experiments, particularly in large cohorts. Several steps were taken to minimize batch effects in this experiment, including using a roboticized protocol to minimize variation in sample preparation within and between plates, consecutively running samples on the mass spectrometer to minimize total experiment run time and associated MS drift, and running all peptides from each nanoparticle on the same mass spectrometer. The impact of batch effects on downstream analysis was limited by sample randomization so any effect would be distributed over the cohort rather than isolated to a specific subset of samples. Batch effects were assessed for in both the experimental and control samples. Our experimental samples were well mixed in PCA space, with only 9% of experimental variation attributable to batching on plates and 1% to duration of sample storage by PVCA, indicating little effect of batching at the plate level or from sample storage duration. Corroborating this, control samples each displayed tight grouping in PCA space by sample type rather than by the plate on which they were processed, again indicating minimal impact of a plate level batching effect. Finally, within each control type, there was very little variation in the number of proteins identified or in their intensity across plates, indicating consistent results across technical replicated processed and analyzed on separate plates. Taken together, these analyses indicate batch effects are not prominent in our dataset.
Comparing the stages of plasma cell dyscrasias within our cohort, we identified several proteins that were significantly more intense in MM compared to the precursor conditions MGUS and SMM. Many of these proteins are plasma cell markers and have been previously reported as significantly higher in BMIF or blood plasma from MM patients than from healthy controls [
25
]. The concordance of our findings with the literature and that the intensities of these plasma cell markers significantly correlated with bone marrow plasma cell burden supports the validity of our findings from this sample preparation method novelly applied to MM BMIF.
A key finding in this study is the link between the low intensity of coagulation factors in BMIF and reduced OS and PFS in MM. Our analysis revealed distinct patient clusters, characterised by globally low, medium, or high intensities of all coagulation factors. Notably, in comparison to the low plasma cell burden comparator group, the high-risk MM group exhibited significantly lower intensity of all coagulation proteins except VWF. Conversely, the low-risk group’s coagulation factor profile was, except for VWF, not significantly different from that of the comparator group. The consistent pattern of reduced coagulation factors suggests that these derangements may arise either from impaired hepatic production or from consumption within the bone marrow microenvironment. As INR and PTT did not differ between coagulation groups, a hepatic origin is less likely, making a localized process in the marrow, or one below the resolving limit of peripheral coagulation assays, more possible. Additionally, low levels of factor 8, which is produced largely in the endothelium, is not consistent with a hepatic origin. Notably, both pro- and anti-coagulant proteins (PROC, PROZ, PROS1, SERPINC1, SERPIND1, SERPINA10), along with coagulation-regulating ECM proteins (tenascin and fibronectin) were reduced in the high-risk group, indicating a dysregulated coagulation milieu rather than a clearly hyper- or hypo- coagulable state. Because fibrin degradation products were not assessed, we cannot determine whether these findings reflect a truly consumptive process, and further studies will be required to clarify the underlying mechanism.
As our analysis profiles BMIF, comprised of a mixed contribution of proteins from malignant plasma cells and other bone marrow resident cells, we could not separately probe the cellular features of the malignancy or its niche that drive the coagulation profiles. Nonetheless, several other proteomics studies have implicated coagulation-related proteins in MM at the cellular level. Dunphy and collaborators found that hemostasis-related proteins are more abundant in bone marrow mononuclear cells (BMNCs) of extramedullary MM, a high-risk MM variant, compared to MM [
23
]. Mohamed and collaborators found that plasma cells in RISS high-risk MM patients differentially expressed proteins involved in platelet degranulation compared to RISS low-risk MM patients [
26
]. In the interactive myeloma dashboard shared in Ramberger and collaborators’ proteogenomic profiling of MM, low expression of SERPINC1 in MM cells is associated with reduced PFS [
24
]. Though our analysis does not discern cell-level protein expression, the high-risk coagulation profile may therefore represent downstream depletion of coagulation factors consequent to the altered expression of pro- and anti-coagulants bone marrow milieu previously reported in MM [
23
,
24
,
26
]. Indeed, activation of coagulation is an important signal in both the development and progression of many cancers and is achieved through the contributions from both malignant and stromal cells [
38
]. Importantly, the hypercoagulability associated with malignancy is recognized to occur independently of conventional coagulation assays (e.g., PTT, INR) and individual coagulation factor levels, highlighting the complexity of prothrombotic mechanisms in this context. Furthermore, in MM, a recent study highlighted the importance of platelet exosomes, released upon platelet activation, in both promoting MM cell proliferation and informing prognosis [
39
]. The emerging importance of coagulation in MM BMIF, and that coagulopathies may arise from either malignant or benign stromal cells, positions BMIF as an important analyte as its assessment probes for coagulopathies regardless of the cell type driving the phenotype.
Our findings complement a recent intracellular MM plasma cell proteogenomic study by Ramberger et al. [
24
], which identified tumor-intrinsic protein signatures linked to prognosis and therapeutic targets. In contrast, our study focuses on the extracellular bone marrow interstitial fluid, revealing a distinct coagulation-related protein signature associated with overall survival. This highlights the added value of fluid-based proteomics in capturing microenvironmental and systemic processes that may influence disease progression and risk stratification in MM.
An important gap in this study is our lack of data on thromboembolic events in our patient cohort. Consequently, the link between the observed BMIF coagulation profiles and thrombosis beyond the bone marrow remains unclear. Indeed, systemic hypercoagulability is well known in MM, with markedly elevated risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) [
40
,
41
]. However, the coagulation profiles identified in BMIF in this study were not reflected in peripheral blood indices (INR, PTT), nor were they explained by the use of antiplatelets or anticoagulants at diagnosis. While INR and PTT are insensitive to moderate fluctuations in factor levels, our findings may therefore indicate a coagulation dysregulation specific to the bone marrow niche. Such changes may impact MM biology through effects on cell adhesion, angiogenesis or immune modulation and could serve as markers of more aggressive disease[
42
]. While anticoagulants are clinically established for VTE prophylaxis and treatment in MM, whether they also exert direct effects on the marrow microenvironment or on MM progression remains unknown. Further investigation into this possibility is warranted to clarify whether anticoagulation may offer therapeutic benefits beyond thrombosis prevention [
43
].
Another limitation of this study is the small sample size of preclinical MM, which restricted our ability to analyze signals specific to the BMIF of MGUS and SMM compared to MM. This also limited our capacity to identify features that distinguish high-risk variants of these precursor conditions. Furthermore, while no association was observed between the coagulation profile and anti-myeloma therapies administered during follow-up, our sample size prevented a detailed exploration of potential interactions between coagulation profiles and individual therapies. Moreover, our survival outcomes were derived predominantly from patients treated with CyBorD, which may limit direct generalisability to locations where alternative induction regimens are used. Nevertheless, because differential expression of PGs was observed pre-treatment, these associations likely reflect underlying disease biology and would be expected to persist across other therapeutic regimens. Additionally, while the identified prognostic coagulation signature was RISS-independent (suggesting independence from high-risk FISH abnormalities included in the RISS) only a subset of our NDMM patients were R-ISS scored, limiting our assessment of the risk conferred by coagulation cluster within R-ISS-scored patients to those of intermediate risk.
Conclusions
This study provides novel insights into multiple myeloma pathology through advanced proteomic characterization. It reveals significant disturbances in coagulation factors within the bone marrow of MM patients, especially in high-risk cases, suggesting local dysregulation of coagulation. These preliminary findings underscore the potential of BMIF coagulation profiling as a valuable biomarker for assessing risk and support the need for further investigation into the therapeutic role of anticoagulants in managing MM.
